subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]
passage: Pema, you want to know how to give a client bad news? Let me tell you about a time I did it well enough. I'm Reena. I was a young woman of twenty-six, so nervous my tea went cold. The migration had failed and the go-live would slip. I named the cause plainly, once. I said sorry once, not five times. Then I put a page on the screen: week one, week two, week three, each with a name beside it, and a promise of a short update every Tuesday and Friday. The client's operations head stopped asking how this could have happened and started asking about week two. They could judge the recovery, not just the problem. That was the whole trick, if you can call it one.

qa.q: On which days did Reena promise updates?
qa.a: Reena promised a short update every Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling before giving the news?
qa.a: Reena was so nervous that the tea went cold.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped the client stay engaged, and why?
qa.a: Putting up a page with weeks and named owners helped, because the client could judge the recovery instead of only dwelling on the problem.

qa.q: How did the client's operations head see the plan?
qa.a: The operations head probably felt steadier, since the plan gave something concrete to ask about and shifted the questions from blame to week two.

grounding: Illustrates giving the cause, one apology and a weekly plan with named owners and regular updates so a client can judge the recovery.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]
passage:
The client's flight to Dubai boarded in fifteen minutes, so Zeenat had one short call to get it right. Ujjwal answered from the airport lounge, clearly distracted.
"The payroll migration will miss the fifteenth," she said. "Our test run found salary records duplicating, because the old system stored overtime in two tables. I'm sorry; we should have caught it earlier."
She didn't repeat the apology. Instead she shared her screen: week one, clean the overtime data, owner Rakesh; week two, a parallel payroll run, owner herself; week three, sign-off with his finance head.
"You'll get a written update every Tuesday and Friday, even if nothing has moved."
Ujjwal was quiet, then asked which week carried the most risk. She told him honestly: week two.
"Fine. Send the plan before I land."

qa.q: Which week did Zeenat say carried the most risk?
qa.a: She told Ujjwal honestly that week two, the parallel payroll run, carried the most risk.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have been feeling as she shared her screen instead of apologising again?
qa.a: She was probably tense under the time pressure but steadier once she moved to the plan; apologising once and then showing concrete weeks let her feel prepared rather than defensive.

qa.q: What else could Zeenat add if the airport call had been cut off halfway?
qa.a: She could send the week-by-week plan in writing straight away with the owners and update days, so Ujjwal could judge the recovery on his own time instead of relying on a rushed call.

qa.q: How does the plan look from Ujjwal's side?
qa.a: Instead of only hearing that payroll is late, he can see who owns each week and when he will hear next, so he can ask about risk and decide whether to trust the recovery.

grounding: It shows a deliverer explaining the cause, apologising once and giving a week-by-week recovery plan with named owners and twice-weekly updates.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]
passage:
The print shop in Andheri had its big press break down on Monday, and by Wednesday Elizabeth knew the conference catalogues would be four days late.
She drove to Farhan's office in Lower Parel rather than emailing. Over a cup of cutting chai, she laid it out: a cracked roller, a spare part coming from Pune, the new delivery date of the twenty-second.
"I'm sorry. This one is on us for relying on one press."
Then she slid across a single printed page. Days one and two, proofs approved at a second shop, owner Elizabeth. Day three, printing, owner Mr. Joshi. Day four, delivery to the venue. Update calls every Monday and Thursday until the event.
Farhan read it twice. "At least I can tell my director something real."
He circled day three and asked for a photo of the first printed sheet.

qa.q: Why were the conference catalogues going to be late?
qa.a: The print shop's big press broke down with a cracked roller, and the spare part was coming from Pune, so the catalogues would be four days late.

qa.q: What does Farhan's comment about telling his director suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He sounds relieved but still under pressure; he was worried about facing his director and felt steadier once he had a concrete plan to pass on.

qa.q: Which other approach could suit Elizabeth if Farhan had been angry and unwilling to meet?
qa.a: She could ask a colleague Farhan already trusts to share the news and the plan with her, because a familiar voice may keep him open to the recovery steps.

qa.q: How would Farhan's day look different if Elizabeth had only emailed that the catalogues were late?
qa.a: He would have a problem with no dates or owners to pass up the chain, so he would likely feel more anxious and have to chase her for answers.

grounding: It shows a supplier naming the cause, apologising once and presenting a dated recovery plan with owners and twice-weekly update calls so the client can judge the recovery.
